field: Has the producer complied with their recycling obligations in accordance with Regulation 40?
finding: Blank for all 428 producers that ARE subject to recycling obligations, and 'N/A' for the 11,650 that are not. The compliance answer is therefore absent for exactly the population it applies to. Not filled in; reported as a gap in the published register.

field: Has the producer submitted a certificate of compliance in accordance with Regulation 41?
finding: Blank for the same 428 rows, for the same reason. Not filled in.
93 rows have no Companies House number. Not all obligated producers are registered companies, so a blank is not necessarily an error. Left alone.

One row is one registration, not one business. 12,078 rows cover 7,925 organisations. Organisation 111484 alone holds 1,275 rows (Specsavers, Visionplus and Hearcare franchise companies), 10.6 per cent of the file, of which exactly one is subject to recycling obligations. Counting rows as producers overstates the population. Key on Producer Registration Number, which is unique across all 12,078 rows.
Each quarterly file holds that quarter alone and is not cumulative, confirmed by comparing Q1 against Q4 tonnages. An annual figure is the sum of four files.

subject: Paper Composting, Wood Composting
finding: Both carry zero in all 51 published values across 2023-2025. The accreditation categories exist in the schema but no tonnage is reported against them. Left in the data rather than dropped, so the absence is visible.

subject: Total PRNs/PERNs issued
finding: Summing the four quarters understates annual evidence issuance by the January window: 9.6 per cent of 2023 issuance, 11.9 per cent of 2024 and 14.5 per cent of 2025. Table 4 of the Q4 file carries the true annual total, and quarters plus January reconciles to it exactly for all 21 year-material pairs.

subject: Glass
finding: pEPR reports one Glass category while the recovery data splits re-melt from other. Any recycling rate per glass stream is therefore not computable from these sources, and a combined glass rate inherits the Paper / Card definitional caveat as well.

Table 2 splits each material's tonnage by agreed protocol, the agreement that fixes what share of a received load counts as packaging. Net received summed over protocols reconciles exactly to Table 1's UK reprocessing figure in all 84 year-quarter-material combinations, which is how the two tables were validated against each other.

subject: 1+2 Mixed
finding: The gross-to-net ratio varies enormously by protocol and is the single most consequential assumption in the dataset. In 2025 steel ran 1,198,621 tonnes gross through accredited reprocessors to yield 69,809 tonnes of packaging evidence, 5.8 per cent overall, and the '1+2 Mixed' protocol alone converts 241,047 tonnes gross into 1,326 tonnes net, 0.6 per cent. Steel packaging evidence is therefore largely a by-product of general scrap processing, and the tonnage credited rests on a protocol-assumed packaging fraction rather than on measured packaging. Glass, wood and the '100% Packaging' protocols sit at the opposite end at 100 per cent.

Table 3 names accredited operators that had not filed their quarterly return at the extraction date: 140 instances across the three years and 63 distinct companies. Non-filing concentrates in Q4 (17, 29 and 23 against 5 to 13 for other quarters) and exporters outnumber reprocessors roughly two to one. Published tonnage for a quarter is therefore incomplete to the extent of these operators' unreported volumes, which the table does not quantify.

subject: Glass Other, Wood
finding: The PRN revenue files state that glass other and wood are not split by operator type, because releasing it would breach EIR Regulation 12(5)(e) on commercially confidential information. The suppression is lawful and permanent, so revenue by accreditation type is unavailable for those two materials.

subject: Exp & Rep
finding: In the waste balance sheet, glass other is reported as a single 'Exp & Rep' row while every other material is split into Exporter and Reprocessor. Glass other therefore cannot be split by stream in that table, although the detail sheet does split it. Left as published.

subject: Wood
finding: Wood carries zero in all 90 exporter values across the nine months. No wood is exported for recycling under accreditation. Kept in the data so the absence is visible.

Outstanding returns rise from 0 in January to 48 in September 2026, because recent months' returns are still arriving. Any month-on-month trend ending at the latest month will understate it. The published figures are provisional by design, not wrong.

subject: Waste balance
finding: The waste balance is tonnage credited during the reporting month, which the regulator describes as issued PRNs plus tonnage eligible for issuance. It is a monthly flow, not a stock, so issuance in a month can exceed that month's credit by drawing on accumulated balance: this happens in 28 of 117 material-month-stream rows. Cumulative credit exceeds cumulative issuance for all seven materials, so there is no inconsistency to correct.

subject: Tonnage recycled
finding: Over January to September 2026 cumulative tonnage recycled EXCEEDS cumulative tonnage received for two materials: glass other by 25,937 tonnes (191,275 recycled against 165,338 received, 15.7 per cent more) and paper and board by 66,015 tonnes (901,168 against 835,154, 7.9 per cent more). Material cannot be recycled before it is received, so the excess is stock held at the start of 2026 and processed during it. This is a measured floor on opening stock for those two materials, not the whole of it, because any stock still unprocessed at the extraction date is not captured. Within single months the same pattern appears in 31 of 63 material-months and is ordinary drawdown; the cumulative figure is the one that carries information.

subject: Average PRN/PERN price per tonne (£)
finding: Average price per tonne spans two orders of magnitude across materials in 2026: paper and board £1.50 to £8.94, plastic £234.09 to £876.30. The cost of discharging an obligation therefore depends overwhelmingly on which material it is in.

subject: Total waste accepted or exported
finding: Despite the folder name, this dataset is NOT exports. The published measure is 'Total Waste Accepted or Exported' — UK reprocessing and export combined. The 2025 final figure of 7,794,043 tonnes matches the quarterly dataset's combined total of 7,795,720 to within 1,677 tonnes, 0.02 per cent, and that gap is explained by extraction date: this file was taken on 10 February 2026 and the quarterly Q4 file on 30 March 2026. To split UK reprocessing from export, use the quarterly dataset, which reports the two separately. Treating this file as export tonnage would overstate exports by roughly a factor of two.

The thirteen sheets per file are CUMULATIVE totals from 1 January to each cut-off date, not monthly increments. Summing the sheets would multiply the year's tonnage roughly sevenfold. The monthly flow is the difference between consecutive snapshots, which is what clean/export_flows_increments_clean.csv provides.

Between 9.9 and 11.6 per cent of each year's final tonnage was not on the database when the compliance year closed: 812,240 tonnes for 2023, 942,811 for 2024 and 882,032 for 2025. By material in 2025 the lag runs from 8.6 per cent for aluminium to 14.3 per cent for wood. This corroborates the January-window finding in the quarterly dataset from a different measure — tonnage entered rather than evidence issued — and means any figure quoted before roughly February of the following year is provisional by about a tenth.

subject: 25_02_10_Rpt_(Recycling_2024_Monthly_Report__01_Jan_2024_-_10_Feb_2025)_(6).xlsx
finding: The 2024 filename carries a '_(6)' suffix added by the browser on download, not by the regulator. Left as downloaded so the file on disk matches the manifest hash; it has no effect on parsing, which reads the compliance year from the 'Recycling_2024_Monthly_Report' portion.

H1, H2 and the annual block are all present in the same sheet, and the annual block is the sum of the two halves. Summing all three would count every tonne twice. Filter to one period before aggregating: period equal to the compliance year is the annual figure.

subject: Glass
finding: pEPR reports a single Glass category while the recovery datasets split re-melt from other. A combined glass recycling rate is computable by summing the two recovery streams; a per-stream rate is not computable from these sources at all. Fibre Composite and Other have no recovery counterpart, so no rate can be computed for them either.

subject: Small producer
finding: Small producers have no 2023 data: the obligation to report was phased in, so 2023 is large producers only. Small producer tonnage is in any case marginal, rising from 34,404 tonnes in 2024 to 82,326 in 2025 against 10.97 million for large producers in 2025, which is 0.7 per cent of the total. A 2023-to-2025 trend on the combined figure would therefore conflate real change with the phase-in.

The recyclability assessment exists for 2025 only, so there is no baseline to compare it against. It drives fee modulation from 2026, and the red-rated share varies enormously by material: wood 98.1 per cent, Other 94.2 per cent and flexible plastic 61.8 per cent against glass at 2.9 per cent and steel at 8.5 per cent. Flexible plastic is the substantial case, at 244,933 tonnes red-rated.

subject: Total Supplied
finding: Packaging placed on the market by large producers fell from 12,146,078 tonnes in 2023 to 11,105,009 in 2024 and 10,970,502 in 2025, a 9.7 per cent decline over two years. Because each year was extracted on a different date, part of that movement may be reporting completeness rather than real change, and the 2023 figure is the stalest.

subject: Large producer
finding: The regulator's recycling obligation estimate is derived from LARGE producer tonnage alone. Multiplying large producer supply by the 2026 target reproduces the published obligation exactly, to 0.00 per cent, for all seven materials; including small producers overshoots by 1.85 per cent for wood and is out for every other material. Small producers report their tonnage but carry no recycling obligation.

subject: UK total recycling obligation
finding: The 2026 statutory obligation totals 7,590,797 tonnes, derived as 2025 placed-on-market tonnage multiplied by the 2026 target for each material. The recovery datasets show the system already evidenced 7,795,720 tonnes of recycling in 2025, so the obligation sits about 2.6 per cent BELOW what was achieved the year before. The two figures use different material taxonomies and are only comparable in aggregate, but at aggregate level the 2026 targets do not require the system to recycle more than it already does. Plastic carries the lowest target at 57 per cent and steel the highest at 81 per cent.

subject: Exp & Rep
finding: Glass other and wood are published as a single combined 'Exp & Rep' row rather than split into exporter and reprocessor. The files state the reason: releasing the split would breach EIR Regulation 12(5)(e) on the confidentiality of commercially sensitive information. The suppression is lawful and permanent, so revenue by operator type is unavailable for those two materials in every year. Any exporter-versus-reprocessor comparison covers five materials, not seven.

subject: 26_03_25_Rpt_(2025_PRN_Revenue_Report).xlsx
finding: The 2025 file carries a stray numeric cell at row 6, column 13, holding 322,471,936 — the grand total copied into an otherwise empty far column. A spreadsheet artefact, not data. The parser reads only the mapped spend columns and reports any numeric value outside them, which is how this was found. It is excluded from the output.

The three files are not laid out identically. The header is on row 1 in 2023 and 2024 and row 2 in 2025. The row order differs: 2023 and 2024 list Reprocessor before Exporter for glass re-melt, paper, plastic and steel, while 2025 lists Exporter first. Nothing is read by row or column position; the header is found by its label and every row is keyed on the material and accreditation type it carries.

Total reported revenue was 595,564,715 pounds in 2023, 291,957,687 in 2024 and 322,471,936 in 2025 — a fall of 51.0 per cent followed by a rise of 10.5 per cent. The trajectory is not a steady decline, and the 2023 figure is nearly double either later year.

Materials sit in columns 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the sheet; column 3 is an empty spacer. Every value is read by its column position against its own table's header row, so a material with no figure leaves a gap rather than shifting the ones after it.

subject: Activity share
finding: The activity shares are the apportionment the regulations fix for who carries the obligation on a given tonne: 6 per cent raw material manufacturing, 9 per cent conversion, 37 per cent pack/filling and 48 per cent selling. They are published as percentages against each activity row and are identical in both years. The import tables use a different split again — 6, 15 and 52 per cent across conversion, pack/filling and selling — which does not sum to 100 and is published that way.

subject: Total recycling obligation
finding: The total recycling obligation was 7,939,063 tonnes for registration year 2023 and 7,901,506 for 2024, a fall of 0.5 per cent. Each is the sum of a general obligation and a material specific one: 481,302 plus 7,457,761 for 2023, and 615,066 plus 7,286,440 for 2024. The general share more than doubled between the two years while the total barely moved.

subject: Number of producers
finding: Producers carrying an obligation fell from 6,968 in 2023 to 6,941 in 2024, and allocation producers from 230 to 193. The published strings also give the split between direct registrants and scheme members — 362 direct of 6,968 in 2023, 318 of 6,941 in 2024 — and are kept whole in value_as_published, since only the leading count is parsed to a number.

There is no 2025 file. This dataset covers registration years 2023 and 2024 only, because the PRN producer obligation regime was replaced by pEPR. For the obligation on the new basis, see the pEPR dataset, which publishes a 2026 obligation of 7,590,797 tonnes — 3.9 per cent below the 2024 figure here. The two are calculated on different bases and the comparison is indicative, not like for like.
